newsitem.title: USA: More chances for seniors to work.
newsitem.headline: More chances for seniors to work.

text.p: Chances for seniors to find work may be improving in today's tight labour market, especially if they're willing to start at the bottom.

"As unemployment in various parts of the country gets down to very low levels, employers are beginning to reach out to people that otherwise would remain out of the labour force, including the elderly and the poor," Labour Secretary Robert Reich told Reuters.
"My basic advice to them is if they are at all interested in getting back into the work force now is the ideal time," he said.
Half the states have opened one-stop career centres that offer job counselling, training, and placement and which are "ideal for people who have been out of the job market," Reich added.

Consultant Cathy Fyock, president of Innovative Management Concepts in Louisville, Ky., and co-author of "Unretirement" (Amacom Books), said, "There's still a lot of bias against hiring seniors but I am seeing large numbers of employers being open to the idea of older adults."

"The good news is that we have actually seen a trend of more (senior) women returning to work," said Deborah Briceland-Betts, executive director of the Older Women's League, a non-profit information and lobbying group based in Washington.
"The bad news is that the jobs that are available are the least attractive ones, service and entry level jobs with no benefits," she said.

One study that supports this view was made of 70 older widows by psychologist Sara Staats of Ohio State University. She found "most of them making $20,000 to $30,000 a year and very few earning as much as $70,000."
James Portwood, human resources professor at Temple University in Philadelphia, said he sees "people hiring senior citizens to work as burger flippers."

Carroll Stephens, management professor at Virginia Polytechnical Institute, in Blacksburg, Va., said she sees older women returning "at temporary low-wage jobs, such as being a bag boy at a supermarket."
Sears, Roebuck & Co., whose 200,000 retail work force counts nearly 70,000 employees age 40 and over, reports seeing a trend of seniors seeking jobs and is hiring them both part- and full-time.
Michael Bass, human resources director, said about 2,400 Sears employees are at least 70 and that they "perform very well."
"We have a number of places in the store where experience and maturity are a real plus and customers have come to expect that."
But seniors seeking full-time jobs usually will not find them overnight.
Ellen Bravo, executive director of 9to5, the National Association of Working Women, thinks that older women who lost their jobs to downsizing "are having a very hard time becoming re-employed."

And David Opten, executive director of Exec-U-Net, a Norwalk, Conn., organisation that helps seniors manage their careers, noted that while people are getting more interviews " I've not seen a significant change" (in hiring).
It still takes senior executives "twice as long" as those under 45 to find work, he said.
The quickest way for seniors to re-enter the job market may be to hire on as a temporary.

Employers are "very favourable" to older workers, "but we can't get enough of them," said Rosemary Maniscalco, president of Uniforce Staffing Services Inc., a Woodbury, N.Y., company that provides temporary employees to companies. "Many only want to work part-time."
About half (54 percent) of those over age 65 who worked in 1994 worked part time, the Bureau of Labour Statistics said.

Olsten Corp., a Melville, N.Y.-based temporary staffing provider, got a "very positive" response from job-hunting seniors last Labour Day when it announced it would have 2 million openings through year-end, said Susan Vassallo, communications director.
"We got lots of retirees and retired military persons, people who had been downsized and are re-entering the work force, as well as parents who took time off to raise children," Vassallo said.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
